scenes.tts: Cells in your body make a protein called H I F 1 alpha. While oxygen is around, they destroy it again within minutes. Why build a protein only to throw it away? It is a transcription factor, a protein that switches on the genes a cell needs when oxygen runs short.
scenes.caption: Cells in your body make a protein called HIF-1α. While oxygen is around, they destroy it again within minutes. Why build a protein only to throw it away? It is a transcription factor, a protein that switches on the genes a cell needs when oxygen runs short.
scenes.visual: A tank for HIF-1α: copies drop in from above and drain out below, so the level stays low. Oxygen dots, a clock and a big Why? appear, then a dashed arrow runs from the tank to a row of genes needed when oxygen runs short.
scenes.narration: Cells in your body make a protein called HIF-1α. While oxygen is around, they destroy it again within minutes. Why build a protein only to throw it away? It is a transcription factor, a protein that switches on the genes a cell needs when oxygen runs short.

scenes.tts: A cell destroys a protein by tagging it with ubiquitin, a small protein. Three enzymes pass the ubiquitin along, called E 1, E 2, and E 3. The E 3 binds the target, so the E 3 decides which protein is tagged. It reads a degron, a mark on the target that tells the system to destroy it. The proteasome, a barrel-shaped protease, then destroys the tagged protein.

scenes.visual: A target protein and a ubiquitin chip; E1, E2 and E3 chips appear and a ubiquitin dot hops along them; the target rises into the E3 cup, a gold degron peg inside it; the tagged target drops into a proteasome barrel and breaks up.
scenes.narration: A cell destroys a protein by tagging it with ubiquitin, a small protein. Three enzymes pass the ubiquitin along, called E1, E2 and E3. The E3 binds the target, so the E3 decides which protein is tagged. It reads a degron, a mark on the target that tells the system to destroy it. The proteasome, a barrel-shaped protease, then destroys the tagged protein.

scenes.tts: Some proteins do not carry a degron all the time. A signal writes it, and for H I F 1 alpha the signal is oxygen. An enzyme called a prolyl hydroxylase needs iron, a small molecule called 2-oxoglutarate, and one molecule of oxygen. With these, it adds a hydroxyl group to one proline of the protein. That hydroxyl is the degron, and the oxygen is used up, like flour in bread.

scenes.visual: A target chip with an empty dashed slot becomes HIF-1α; a signal chip becomes oxygen; the prolyl hydroxylase takes in iron, 2-oxoglutarate and oxygen, a gold OH badge lands on the slot and is named the degron, and the oxygen chip is used up.

An enzyme called a prolyl hydroxylase needs iron, a small molecule called 2-oxoglutarate, and one molecule of oxygen. With these, it adds a hydroxyl group to one proline of the protein. scenes.tts: V H L is the part of an E 3 that grips the hydroxylated proline. A short piece of H I F 1 alpha, made with the hydroxyl in place, bound V H L tightly. The same piece with an ordinary proline did not. So the hydroxyl itself is the mark. Held by V H L, H I F 1 alpha gets a ubiquitin chain, and the proteasome destroys it.
scenes.caption: VHL is the part of an E3 that grips the hydroxylated proline. A short piece of HIF-1α, made with the hydroxyl in place, bound VHL tightly. The same piece with an ordinary proline did not. So the hydroxyl itself is the mark. Held by VHL, HIF-1α gets a ubiquitin chain, and the proteasome destroys it.
scenes.visual: The VHL cup closes on the OH badge of HIF-1α; a second row shows a plain proline that the cup cannot grip; the OH is named the mark; then a ubiquitin chain grows on HIF-1α, which drops into the proteasome.
scenes.narration: VHL is the part of an E3 that grips the hydroxylated proline. A short piece of HIF-1α, made with the hydroxyl in place, bound VHL tightly. The same piece with an ordinary proline did not. So the hydroxyl itself is the mark. Held by VHL, HIF-1α gets a ubiquitin chain, and the proteasome destroys it.

scenes.tts: Now oxygen falls. The enzyme finishes its reaction less often, so fewer prolines get a hydroxyl. V H L has less to grip, and H I F 1 alpha is spared. It builds up and pairs with a partner protein called A R N T. Together they switch on genes such as V E G F, a growth factor that drives new blood vessels.
scenes.caption: Now oxygen falls. The enzyme finishes its reaction less often, so fewer prolines get a hydroxyl. VHL has less to grip, and HIF-1α is spared. It builds up and pairs with a partner protein called ARNT. Together they switch on genes such as VEGF, a growth factor that drives new blood vessels.
scenes.visual: Oxygen thins out; OH badges vanish from two of three HIF-1α copies and their VHL cups open; the two spared copies pour into the tank and the level climbs; HIF-1α pairs with ARNT and two genes, one named VEGF, turn green.
scenes.narration: Now oxygen falls. The enzyme finishes its reaction less often, so fewer prolines get a hydroxyl. VHL has less to grip, and HIF-1α is spared. It builds up and pairs with a partner protein called ARNT. Together they switch on genes such as VEGF, a growth factor that drives new blood vessels.

scenes.tts: So why make the protein just to destroy it? The cell keeps making it, so a fall in oxygen only has to spare it. Making it on demand would mean waiting for transcription and translation, which takes tens of minutes to hours. And when oxygen returns, the protein disappears within minutes. Keep this rule: a signal can write the destruction mark, and here oxygen writes it.
scenes.visual: A plot of the HIF-1α level against time: flat, a rise when oxygen falls, a dashed wait for an on-demand route, a fast fall when oxygen returns; then oxygen becomes the mark that sends the protein to the proteasome.
